title: Nested Conditions and Decision Structure
learningObjectives: Describe how a condition can contain or lead to another condition.
Trace nested if/else decision paths in order.
Choose between nested conditions and combined logical expressions.
Design readable decision structures for multi-step requirements.
Recognize common errors such as misplaced else branches and excessive nesting.

understand.concept: Nested conditions are decision structures in which one decision is placed inside another. The inner decision is evaluated only when execution reaches it. Each branch can contain another decision, creating multiple paths through a program.
understand.whyItMatters: Many tasks require checking a primary rule first and then checking details only when that rule passes. Nesting can express this sequence, but poorly organized branches become hard to read, test and maintain.
understand.analogy: At a building entrance, security first checks whether a person has an invitation. Only if the invitation is valid does security check whether the person is on today's guest list. The second check is nested inside the first decision.
understand.analogyLimit: Real procedures can have exceptions and parallel checks. This simple analogy models only a small decision process.

explain.narrative: A nested if statement places an if/else decision inside an outer if or else branch. The outer condition controls whether the inner condition is reached. Trace execution from top to bottom and track the active branch. In JavaScript, braces are recommended even for single statements because they make branch boundaries clear. An else belongs to the nearest unmatched if; missing braces can create confusing dangling-else behaviour. Nesting is useful when the second check depends on the first, but many levels can become difficult to maintain. Consider early returns, helper functions or a clearly grouped logical expression. Do not change a rule's meaning merely to reduce indentation.

examples.title: Outer condition gates inner condition
examples.code: const hasInvite = true; const isOnList = false; if (hasInvite) { if (isOnList) { console.log('Welcome'); } else { console.log('Check guest list'); } } else { console.log('No entry'); }
examples.explanation: The invitation check passes, so the inner guest-list check runs and selects its else branch.

examples.title: Nested else path
examples.code: const isMember = false; const hasTrial = true; if (isMember) { console.log('Member access'); } else { if (hasTrial) { console.log('Trial access'); } else { console.log('Denied'); } }
examples.explanation: The outer condition is false, so the inner trial check in its else branch is evaluated.

examples.title: Three decision outcomes
examples.code: const score = 85; if (score >= 90) { console.log('Excellent'); } else { if (score >= 70) { console.log('Pass'); } else { console.log('Retry'); } }
examples.explanation: The first threshold fails, then the second condition succeeds.

examples.title: Inner decision is skipped
examples.code: const isLoggedIn = false; const isAdmin = true; if (isLoggedIn) { if (isAdmin) { console.log('Admin panel'); } else { console.log('User page'); } } else { console.log('Sign in'); }
examples.explanation: The outer condition is false, so the inner administrator condition is never evaluated.

examples.title: Clear branch ownership
examples.code: const hasAccount = true; const isVerified = false; if (hasAccount) { if (isVerified) { console.log('Verified'); } else { console.log('Verify account'); } } else { console.log('Create account'); }
examples.explanation: Braces show which else belongs to the inner and outer if statements.

guidedTask.title: Guided: Two-step access check
guidedTask.instructions: First check whether the user is signed in. If they are, check whether their account is verified. Produce three outcomes: Sign in, Verify account, and Access granted.
steps: Inside its true branch, check verification.
Add an else for each decision.
Test all three outcomes by changing the values.
guidedTask.starterCode: const signedIn = true; const verified = false; if (signedIn) { if (verified) { console.log('Access granted'); } else { console.log('Verify account'); } } else { console.log('Sign in'); }

independentTask.title: Independent: Discount decision
independentTask.instructions: If a customer is a member, check whether the purchase is at least 1000 and grant a large discount; otherwise grant a member's small discount. If not a member, check whether the purchase is at least 2000 and grant a non-member discount; otherwise no discount.
requirements: Use nested conditions for both membership paths.
Create a distinct output for each outcome.
Test at least four membership and purchase combinations.
Draw or describe the decision paths.

hints: Start by identifying the first decision that separates paths.
Indent the inner decision under the branch that owns it.
An inner condition is reached only if its outer branch executes.
Use braces to make branch boundaries visible.
Test one case for each final outcome.
If nesting becomes too deep, consider a clearer structure or helper function.

questions.prompt: When is an inner nested condition evaluated?
options: Only when execution reaches it through the outer branch
questions.answer: Only when execution reaches it through the outer branch
questions.explanation: The inner decision is reached only when its containing branch executes.

questions.prompt: What do braces around nested branches help prevent?
options: Confusing branch boundaries and else association
questions.answer: Confusing branch boundaries and else association

questions.prompt: What should be done when nested decision levels become difficult to read?
options: Refactor into a clearer structure or helper function
Add more indentation without changing logic
questions.answer: Refactor into a clearer structure or helper function
questions.explanation: Refactoring can improve readability while preserving the rules.

questions.prompt: If an outer condition is false and its inner check is inside that branch, what happens?
questions.explanation: Execution follows the outer condition's selected path.

questions.prompt: Why trace nested conditions step by step?
options: To identify the actual path and outcome
questions.answer: To identify the actual path and outcome
questions.explanation: Tracing reveals which checks run and which branch produces the result.
